paras: The lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman took place on the night of Tuesday, November 27, 1888, when white men took the two Black men from a convict stockade near Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, and, by most accounts, drowned them in the Broad River. The same party whipped two other Black people, Hulda or Huldah Smith and a male relative. Dispatches called it a "race war" arising from a cotton dispute and an alleged insult to a white woman, and the Augusta Chronicle denounced it as "crimes against civilization and Christianity."

Smith was a tenant on the place of J. E. Bramlet (or Bramlett), a Baptist clergyman, while E. B. Cade, a white storekeeper, supplied him against payment in cotton. According to a Washington, Georgia, dispatch, Mrs. Bramlet refused Smith a team to haul his cotton while her husband was away, Smith and his wife were said to have "addressed abusive language" to her, and Cade lent the team instead. An earlier Savannah paragraph gave Smith's claim that Bramlett had let him gin the bale where he wished, while the Lincolnton News said negroes had taken the cotton-house keys from Mrs. Bramlett at pistol point.

Mrs. Bramlet swore out a warrant, and the Washington account says Smith, found with Coleman and three other armed men, attacked a bailiff's posse with an iron wedge and was shot and wounded; the New-York Tribune said the posse was driven off by "a sharp volley of musketry." Cade signed the men's bonds, a rumor that he had armed 150 Black men brought armed whites to the scene, and Smith and Coleman were rearrested and held in Henry Hill's convict stockade "for safe keeping."

On Tuesday night a party of men took Smith and Coleman from the stockade to the Broad River. The Tribune's correspondent wrote that the two "howled and pleaded for mercy" before they were bound, weighted with rocks tied round their necks, and thrown in from a bluff, as the Evening World described the spot. The lynchers then whipped Hulden Smith and a male relative "until they were nearly dead," according to the Sun, and ordered them to leave.

Black residents were reported arming, and whites appealed to Governor Gordon for protection. A Washington dispatch said the people of Wilkes did not endorse the drowning and favored a full investigation. Later a posse summoned by Sheriff Calloway dragged the river and found no trace of the bodies, and by December 27 the whipped woman and boy had about recovered and the trouble was thought ended. No report of an inquest, arrests or trial appears in the coverage.

The New York Evening World broke the story on December 1 as "Lynched by Drowning," saying the men had been "insulting white ladies" and threatening "respectable citizens." An Atlanta wire ran in the Sun, in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer as "Drowned Like Kittens," and in Sacramento as "The Georgia Race War." The longer Washington dispatch, which traced the killings to the cotton dispute, appeared in the Sun as "Race War in Georgia" and later in Wichita and Newberry, South Carolina, while the Evening World recast the affair as a white men's feud: "It Is Mr. Cade's Turn to Kill."

Weekly briefs in Kentucky, Missouri and Michigan reduced the story to two men who insulted a white woman and were thrown alive into a river. The Augusta Chronicle, reprinted in the Indianapolis Journal as "An Awakening Conscience," said the men were not charged with crimes calling for summary punishment and urged Governor Gordon to act.
The Cleveland Gazette, a Black weekly, printed the Atlanta version on December 22 without comment, opening with the excitement of "the Afro-Americans of Wilkes County."

The lynching party numbered forty in the Washington dispatch, two hundred in the Richmond Democrat, and three hundred in the Atlanta and Tribune reports. The Washington dispatch also noted reports that the men were shot or concealed, and the fruitless dragging left the manner of death unconfirmed. The Elberton report said the men were taken "from their home" and named the whipped pair Hulda Coleman and Jim Smith, while the Tribune named the man John Smith.

reader.title: Lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman
bases: A party of armed white men took two Black men from a convict stockade and drowned them, and whipped two others (A6, A9, A10).

A party of forty to three hundred men took Smith and Coleman from custody and drowned them for an alleged insult to a white woman and resistance to arrest (A6, A9, A2); the bodies were never found and one report mentions they may have been shot or concealed (A10, A19), but every account has them killed by the mob.
Independent Elberton, Atlanta and Washington, Ga., reports agree two men were taken and killed by a mob (A2, A3, A6, A9); the manner of death is disputed and the bodies were not recovered (A10, A19).

accounts.label: Elberton special
accounts.gist: A posse of citizens took Smith and Coleman from their home and drowned them, and whipped Hulda Coleman and Jim Smith, because they had insulted white ladies and threatened citizens.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Two negroes insulted Mrs. Jane Bramlett and fired on officers; 300 armed men threw them into the river with rocks; a young white man fled; Black residents armed.

accounts.label: Washington, Ga., dispatch
accounts.gist: A cotton and supply dispute among Cade, Bramlet and Smith led to a warrant, Smith's shooting at arrest, bail by Cade, rearrest to Hill's stockade, and drowning by forty men; also reports of shooting or concealment.

accounts.label: Lincolnton News
accounts.gist: Before the lynching: negroes took cotton-house keys from Mrs. Bramlett at pistol point, sold the cotton, and fled armed; a posse scoured the woods.

accounts.label: Evening World feud version
accounts.gist: The killings were the result of a feud between Bramlett and Cade; the lynchers meant to kill Cade too.

framing.detail: The Elberton special's headline 'Two Negroes Suffer for Insulting Ladies' and its closing line on threats against 'respectable citizens' gave the mob's reasons as fact.
'The Georgia Race War' and 'Drowned Like Kittens' carried the Atlanta wire with no comment.
The Sun's 'Race War in Georgia' gave a detailed narrative blaming the dispute on Cade and Smith while reporting Wilkes opinion against the drowning.
The Lincolnton News called the accused 'black scoundrels' and warned of 'a terrible retribution'.
The Augusta Chronicle (via the Indianapolis Journal, 'An Awakening Conscience') called the drownings 'barbarities' and urged Gov. Gordon to punish the lynchers.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the wire brief, reframed around 'the Afro-Americans of Wilkes County', without comment.

conflicts.note: Most reports state drowning as fact; no body was recovered.
The Washington dispatch, which claims 'careful investigation', gives forty; 300 may describe the armed whites who gathered earlier.
The later, more detailed reports agree on the stockade.

record_check.dossier: Four people: Tim Smith and John Coleman (killed); Hulda/Huldah/Hulden Smith and Jim (or John) Smith (whipped). 'Joe Coleman' and 'Hulda Coleman' are variant names, not further victims.
Washington is the dateline; the stockade and drowning were on the Broad River near Danburg, Wilkes County.
A lynching party/mob of 40-300 men; the posse was the bailiff's earlier arrest party (the Elberton report alone calls the lynchers a 'posse of citizens').
2 whipped by the lynchers; Smith had also been shot by the arresting posse before the lynching.

record_check.record: said to have insulted white ladies and threatened citizens
record_check.dossier: Also: dispute over removing cotton, abusive language to Mrs. Bramlet, armed resistance to arrest; one report of taking cotton-house keys at pistol point.

record_check.record: Forty men took ... Black tenants held in a convict stockade
record_check.dossier: Only Smith is described as a tenant; mob size also given as 200 or 300; bodies never found.

info: Tuesday night, November 27, 1888 ("Tuesday night" in reports of Dec. 1-4)
Convict stockade of Henry Hill (Hills; 'Honey Hill' in the Tribune) and the Broad River near Danburg, near the Lincoln county line
Tim Smith and John Coleman (Black) killed; Hulda/Huldah/Hulden Smith and a male relative (Jim or John Smith) whipped
Accused of insulting Mrs. Bramlet(t) during a dispute over removing cotton, of resisting arrest and firing on or attacking officers, and of threatening to shoot and burn out citizens
White men of the neighborhood; Bramlett said to have rallied his neighbors; none named as lynchers
Whipped woman and boy recovered; trouble thought at an end by late December; Cade remained away
